snip.t: Clotting: Factors V, VII, VIII, IX, X, XII, von Willebrand factor and fibrinogen (doubles) rise; antithrombin III and protein S fall; fibrinolysis is reduced — A hypercoagulable state: protects against postpartum haemorrhage but raises the risk of venous thromboembolism
This is known as​ Thrombophilia (Hypercoagulable state)​.

The hypercoagulable state is due to loss of
clotting factors (e.g. antithrombin) in the urine and an increase in hepatic production of fibrinogen.
Prolonged bed rest should be avoided, as thromboembolism is very common (particularly in
membranous nephropathy).

Studies to delineate a specific underlying hypercoagulable state are recommended.\nAnticoagulation therapy in children with thrombotic events appears to be effective—heparin, low-molecular-weight heparin, and warfarin are therapeutic options.
Antithrombin III and protein C/S: Urinary loss of these anticoagulants in nephrotic syndrome explains the hypercoagulable state and risk of venous thromboembolism.

qs.q: A patient with advanced pancreatic cancer develops migratory thrombophlebitis, a hypercoagulable state known as Trousseau syndrome. This condition is most characteristically associated with which tumor?
qs.e: Trousseau syndrome, or migratory thrombophlebitis, is associated with tumor hypercoagulability seen in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma. Benign lesions like serous cystadenomas do not typically present with systemic paraneoplastic clotting disorders.
qs.s: Pancreatic Disorders: A Comprehensive Review — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which natural anticoagulant is physiologically reduced in pregnancy, contributing to a hypercoagulable state?
qs.e: Free Protein S levels fall in pregnancy due to increased binding protein, reducing its anticoagulant activity and contributing to venous thromboembolism risk.

ai.title: Hypercoagulable State
ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: A hypercoagulable state is an imbalance favouring clot formation, seen in infections, malignancy, pregnancy and inherited defects. It raises the risk of venous thromboembolism and arterial events.

sections.p: A hypercoagulable state is characterised by increased pro‑coagulant factors (VII, VIII, X, fibrinogen) and decreased anticoagulants (antithrombin, protein C/S). Diagnosis is clinical plus laboratory confirmation.

faq.q: Why is LMWH preferred over warfarin in acute VTE?
faq.a: LMWH has predictable pharmacokinetics, no dietary restrictions, and lower bleeding risk in the first weeks.

faq.q: What is the role of antithrombin III in nephrotic syndrome?
faq.a: Urinary loss of antithrombin III reduces anticoagulant activity, favouring clot formation.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman with recurrent miscarriages presents with a new calf pain – what is the first investigation and why? — Ultrasound Doppler to confirm DVT; rule out underlying thrombophilia with protein C/S, antithrombin, and factor V Leiden.

A patient on warfarin develops a sudden headache and vision loss – what is the likely complication and immediate management? — Intracranial haemorrhage; stop warfarin, give vitamin K and reverse with PCC.
A 45‑year‑old man with HIV on ART presents with sudden dyspnoea – what is the differential and first test? — Pulmonary embolism; CT pulmonary angiogram or V/Q scan if CT unavailable.

An elderly patient with nephrotic syndrome develops a limb swelling – what is the pathophysiology and treatment? — Loss of antithrombin III leads to hypercoagulability; treat with LMWH and manage nephrotic syndrome.
A pregnant woman on LMWH develops a rash and bruising – what is the concern and how to address it? — Possible heparin‑induced thrombocytopenia; check platelet count, stop LMWH, switch to argatroban.
A child with sickle cell disease has a sudden chest pain – what is the likely event and how to confirm? — Pulmonary embolism; confirm with CT pulmonary angiogram or V/Q scan if CT not available.
